main.title: Napple Tale: Arsia in Daydream
main.subtitle: A mistake between worlds
main.summary: Napple Tale: Arsia in Daydream is Chime's platform adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 19 October 2000.

cards.heading: A mistake between worlds
cards.text: Napple Tale: Arsia in Daydream is Chime's platform adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 19 October 2000. Porch Arsia is taken to Napple World by mistake when the spirit guide Straynap confuses her with another target. Six Petals escape from her body into the world's separate seasons, and recovering them becomes her route home. The setting lies between ordinary life and a deeper dream, giving the journey a gentle strangeness. Yoko Kanno composed the music for an adventure that links side-view platform stages with the everyday concerns of its town.

cards.heading: Seasons beyond the town
cards.text: Napple Town forms a fully three-dimensional hub where Porch meets inhabitants and helps with their problems. Routes from the town lead into stages associated with spring, summer, autumn and winter, turning seasons into places that can be visited. Porch uses a swinging weapon, double jumps and a spinning attack to move through those routes and fight enemies. Bosses wait at the end of the stages. The change between town and course gives the player a repeated rhythm: learn what somebody needs, then head into another part of the dream to continue the search.

cards.heading: Small problems in a dream
cards.text: Enemies can leave recipe pieces and other items, with recipes identifying four ingredients that combine into a Paffet. Collection therefore supports another form of making things within the world, alongside the tasks undertaken for its residents. Porch's health is represented by petals, keeping even the interface connected to the story's imagery. Straynap accompanies the journey as an imperfect guide to the dream's rules. The town's personal problems and the separate seasonal landscapes give the search a welcoming scale, allowing the adventure to move between a fantastical destination and a small favour for somebody nearby.

main.title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2
main.summary: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 is a real-time strategy video game released for Microsoft Windows on October 25, 2000, as the follow-up to Command & Conquer: Red Alert.

cards.heading: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2
cards.text: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 is a real-time strategy video game released for Microsoft Windows on October 25, 2000, as the follow-up to Command & Conquer: Red Alert. Red Alert 2 picks up after the Allied campaign of the first game. Its expansion pack is Command & Conquer: Yuri's Revenge, released a year later in 2001. Red Alert 2 was principally developed by Westwood Pacific in collaboration with Westwood Studios.

cards.heading: Allies, Soviets and live-action campaigns
cards.text: Command and Conquer: Red Alert 2 contains two playable factions, the Soviets and the Allies, which both previously appeared in Command & Conquer: Red Alert. Separate Allied and Soviet campaigns follow alternative outcomes of the conflict. Like its predecessor, Red Alert 2 features a large amount of full-motion video cutscenes between missions and during gameplay, with an ensemble cast including Ray Wise, Udo Kier, Kari Wuhrer, and Barry Corbin.

cards.heading: Success leads to Red Alert 3
cards.text: Red Alert 2 was a commercial and critical success, receiving a rating of 86% from GameRankings. It released with a collector's edition. A sequel, Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3, was released in 2008.

main.title: L.O.L.: Lack of Love
main.subtitle: Life on a changing planet
main.summary: L.O.L.: Lack of Love is Love-de-Lic's life simulation, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 2 November 2000.

cards.heading: Life on a changing planet
cards.text: L.O.L.: Lack of Love is Love-de-Lic's life simulation, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 2 November 2000. The player controls a creature on an alien planet being transformed by machines. Staying alive involves finding relationships with other life forms and adapting to the changing environment. Director Kenichi Nishi and composer Ryuichi Sakamoto developed the project around ideas associated with the Gaia hypothesis, which considers the interactions between life and its surroundings. The game presents those concerns through the creature's immediate needs and encounters rather than a conventional sequence of missions.

cards.heading: Learning through other creatures
cards.text: Communicating with other creatures and helping them establishes symbiotic relationships that allow the protagonist to change form. Food, sleep and other bodily needs also shape survival, with very little conventional interface separating the player from the environment. Progress comes from observing what another creature is doing and finding a useful way to respond. An encounter may provide help or sustenance, but it also belongs to a larger network of living things. Learning that network changes what the small protagonist can become and where it can continue to survive.

cards.heading: An ecosystem as the adventure
cards.text: Sakamoto's music supports the unfamiliar landscape while the lack of a prominent display leaves attention on behaviour and surroundings. The project followed Moon and UFO in Love-de-Lic's short history, sharing an interest in actions outside conventional combat and conquest. Its Japanese-only commercial release limited the original audience, with a fan translation arriving much later. The central idea remains direct in play: the creature develops through contact with others, making care, observation and dependence into the means of moving through a world whose future is being altered around it.

main.title: Metropolis Street Racer
main.subtitle: Driving with something to prove
main.summary: Metropolis Street Racer is Bizarre Creations' racing game, first released for Dreamcast in the United Kingdom on 3 November 2000.

cards.heading: Driving with something to prove
cards.text: Metropolis Street Racer is Bizarre Creations' racing game, first released for Dreamcast in the United Kingdom on 3 November 2000. Its routes run through recreations of London, Tokyo and San Francisco, with challenges that reward stylish driving as well as speed. The Kudos system measures that performance, turning a well-controlled slide or a clean finish into progress towards another event. Streets are closed into different courses within the cities, giving familiar junctions new uses as the campaign advances. Winning means showing command of the car, not merely reaching the next corner first.

cards.heading: The price of a stylish corner
cards.text: Challenges award Kudos for completing their objectives and for the way the player drives. Drifting can increase the total, while collisions with scenery or other cars can reduce it. The player can also make certain tasks harder, such as reducing a time allowance, to increase the potential reward. That choice makes difficulty part of preparing the attempt. A spectacular corner becomes worthwhile only if it can be completed cleanly, so the scoring system repeatedly asks whether the extra risk will improve the run or undo its earlier progress.

cards.heading: Three cities, nine radio stations
cards.text: The console's clock determines the time of day in each city, giving a drive through Tokyo a different light from one through London. Richard Jacques composed music for nine fictional radio stations, three associated with each location. Progress unlocks cars and courses for additional modes, extending the use of the city routes. Bizarre later developed Project Gotham Racing for Xbox from related ideas. Metropolis Street Racer established the central relationship that made those ideas distinctive: the road measures speed, while Kudos gives precision and style a second, persistent value.

main.title: Crash Bash
main.summary: Crates, pogo sticks and polar bears turn Crash's familiar cast into four rivals sharing the same arena.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Crash Bash is a 2000 PlayStation party game developed by Eurocom in association with Cerny Games. Aku Aku and Uka Uka settle their rivalry through a contest between familiar heroes and villains. The series' crates, characters and cartoon violence become the material for short arena games, with up to four players sharing a screen.

cards.heading: A crate is also a weapon
cards.text: In Crate Crush, a wooden box becomes something to throw at another player. Picking it up leaves a moment in which a rival can approach, while an explosive crate makes the same action more dangerous. A kick can interrupt someone before the throw lands. The arena keeps all four opponents close enough to interfere, so survival depends on watching the other characters as carefully as the nearest supply of ammunition. Variations change the ground and hazards while keeping that argument over space intact.

cards.heading: Colour the floor, collect the points
cards.text: Pogo Painter turns movement into a claim on the floor. Each bounce colours a square, but points arrive when the player reaches a collecting crate. Covering a large area is tempting; leaving it uncollected gives opponents time to interfere. Missiles and speed boosts can help break another player's rhythm or extend a run. Because the board remains visible beneath everyone, the next target is easy to understand even as several competing trails spread across it.

cards.heading: Win together, then try again
cards.text: Adventure links the arenas through warp rooms and can be played alone or with a partner. Winning a trophy opens further challenges in the same event, where a gem or crystal introduces another condition to overcome. A familiar arena can therefore demand a different approach on the return visit. Battle and Tournament provide shorter ways to gather a group, with a PlayStation Multitap supporting four human players. The same small spaces work both as tests against the computer and as noisy contests between friends.

main.title: Counter-Strike
main.summary: Counter-Strike (also known as Half-Life: Counter-Strike or Counter-Strike 1.6) is a 2000 tactical first-person shooter game developed by Valve Corporation and published by Sierra Studios.

cards.heading: A tactical shooter becomes a commercial release
cards.text: Counter-Strike (also known as Half-Life: Counter-Strike or Counter-Strike 1.6) is a 2000 tactical first-person shooter game developed by Valve Corporation and published by Sierra Studios. It is the first installment in the Counter-Strike series.

cards.heading: Objectives, equipment and the end of a round
cards.text: The game pits two teams—the Counter-Terrorists and Terrorists—against each other in objective-based game modes. The most common objectives are bomb defusal and hostage rescue, each played on designated maps. Players begin with a knife and pistol, and they can purchase more advanced weapons and equipment with money earned through eliminating enemies or accomplishing goals. Once eliminated, players do not respawn until the end of the round.

cards.heading: A Half-Life modification meets Valve
cards.text: Minh Le and Jess Cliffe planned a game based on counter-terrorism in 1998 with development beginning the following year when the first few beta versions were released. Their initial version of the game started as a modification for Half-Life and gained significant popularity and interest, which attracted Valve. Valve went on to acquire the game's intellectual property and announced a partnership with Le and Cliffe. After finishing development, Counter-Strike was released by Valve for Microsoft Windows in November 2000. Several remakes and ports were released on Xbox, as well as OS X and Linux.

cards.heading: Team play becomes a continuing series
cards.text: Since its release, Counter-Strike received positive reviews from critics who praised the gameplay and its emphasis on teamwork and strategy. It has been called one of the most influential first-person shooters and noted for its realistic and tactical approach to counter-terrorism. The game became a major hit, selling millions of copies. Because of this success, multiple subsequent installments were released. The first of these was Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, a single-player campaign released in 2004, which was received with mixed reviews. Counter-Strike: Source came out later that year, which ran on Valve's Source engine, offering improved visuals and physics. In 2012, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive was launched, giving the franchise new game modes and better matchmaking. Counter-Strike 2, developed in the Source 2 engine, was released in 2023 as an update to Global Offensive.

main.title: WWF SmackDown! 2: Know Your Role
main.subtitle: The wrestling show continues between matches
main.summary: WWF SmackDown! 2: Know Your Role is Yuke's PlayStation wrestling game, released in North America on 20 November 2000. It expands the first SmackDown! with a larger roster and a Season Mode that places matches within an ongoing wrestling programme. Familiar WWF performers enter a schedule of rivalries, alliances and backstage encounters rather than appearing only in isolated bouts. The player chooses a wrestler and works through that changing context, with the television presentation helping connect the action in the ring to the personalities whose conflicts make the next match matter.

cards.heading: The wrestling show continues between matches
cards.text: WWF SmackDown! 2: Know Your Role is Yuke's PlayStation wrestling game, released in North America on 20 November 2000. It expands the first SmackDown! with a larger roster and a Season Mode that places matches within an ongoing wrestling programme. Familiar WWF performers enter a schedule of rivalries, alliances and backstage encounters rather than appearing only in isolated bouts. The player chooses a wrestler and works through that changing context, with the television presentation helping connect the action in the ring to the personalities whose conflicts make the next match matter.

cards.heading: Create someone who can belong to the roster
cards.text: Character creation lets the player assemble a wrestler's appearance and moves, while stable creation provides a way to organise groups. Those choices extend participation beyond selecting a famous performer from a menu. In the ring, the accessible controls favour quick exchanges and the spectacle of recognisable moves. Different match arrangements and backstage locations change the surroundings in which a rivalry can continue. The player can therefore approach the game as a succession of competitive bouts or as the construction of a wrestling personality whose actions become part of the season's developing show.

cards.heading: A large sequel near the end of PlayStation's reign
cards.text: Know Your Role arrived only months after the first game and became one of the most successful wrestling releases of its generation, selling more than three million copies. Its substantial Season Mode also made loading times a recurring part of the experience. The next main SmackDown! moved to PlayStation 2 with Just Bring It. This entry captured the WWF's Attitude Era through its roster and the breadth of its wrestling programme, offering a console version of the attraction that extends beyond any single match: the sense that the next episode will continue a familiar, unruly world.

main.title: Mario Party 3
main.summary: Mario Party 3 is a 2000 party video game developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.text: Mario Party 3 is a 2000 party video game developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. The third installment in the Mario Party series, it was first released in Japan on December 7, 2000, in North America on May 7, 2001, in Australia on September 3, 2001, and in Europe on November 16, 2001. As with the previous installments, the player chooses between eight playable characters: Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Yoshi, Wario, and Donkey Kong from the first two games, alongside newcomers Princess Daisy and Waluigi. The game introduces duel maps, where two players try to lower each other's stamina to zero using non-player characters such as Chain Chomps.

Mario Party 3 received generally mixed reviews, with critics divided on its new minigames and gameplay features, and whether it was a meaningful improvement over its predecessors. It was a commercial success, with over 1 million copies sold worldwide, making it one of the best-selling Nintendo 64 games. The game was the final first-party Nintendo 64 title released in North America. It was followed by Mario Party 4 for the GameCube in 2002. Content from Mario Party 3 was remastered as part of Mario Party: The Top 100 (2017) for the Nintendo 3DS and Mario Party Superstars (2021) for the Nintendo Switch. The game received its first official re-release on the Nintendo Classics service on October 27, 2023.

main.title: Dark Cloud
main.subtitle: A village carried in a stone
main.summary: Dark Cloud is Level-5's action role-playing game for PlayStation 2, first released in Japan on 14 December 2000. After the Dark Genie destroys his village, Toan receives a magical stone that lets him recover what has vanished. He enters dungeons to find the people, buildings and belongings needed to rebuild the surface. This gives the adventure two connected activities: fighting through underground floors and arranging the community above them. A successful expedition brings back another piece of a place the player can gradually recognise as home.

cards.heading: A village carried in a stone
cards.text: Dark Cloud is Level-5's action role-playing game for PlayStation 2, first released in Japan on 14 December 2000. After the Dark Genie destroys his village, Toan receives a magical stone that lets him recover what has vanished. He enters dungeons to find the people, buildings and belongings needed to rebuild the surface. This gives the adventure two connected activities: fighting through underground floors and arranging the community above them. A successful expedition brings back another piece of a place the player can gradually recognise as home.

cards.heading: Bring the town back together
cards.text: The Georama system lets the player place recovered buildings and restore the objects around them. Residents also have requests about their surroundings, so rebuilding involves listening as well as choosing an attractive arrangement. A house placed in one position may satisfy someone who wants a particular neighbour or view. Returning from the dungeon changes the town, and talking to the people there supplies another reason to venture back underground. Recovery becomes visible in the streets rather than remaining a list of completed objectives in a menu.

cards.heading: Weapons that grow with their owners
cards.text: Inside the dungeons, combat happens in real time and the party gradually gains characters with different weapons and abilities. Equipment develops through use and can be strengthened, making a familiar weapon something worth maintaining. Procedurally arranged floors offer new routes through repeated expeditions, although that repetition also drew criticism. Akihiro Hino directed the project at the young Level-5 studio, with music by Tomohito Nishiura. Its combination of dungeon exploration and reconstruction continued in Dark Chronicle, released in Japan in 2002 and known in North America as Dark Cloud 2.

main.title: Pokémon Crystal Version
main.subtitle: Johto gains a new traveller and a story around Suicune
main.summary: Pokémon Crystal revisits the Johto adventure of Gold and Silver on Game Boy Color. Game Freak added a choice of player character, animated battle entrances and a storyline following the legendary Suicune. Released in Japan on 14 December 2000, it keeps the journey from a first partner to the Gym challenge while giving familiar places another reason to return.

cards.heading: Another journey through Johto
cards.text: Pokémon Crystal revisits the Johto adventure of Gold and Silver on Game Boy Color. Game Freak added a choice of player character, animated battle entrances and a storyline following the legendary Suicune. Released in Japan on 14 December 2000, it keeps the journey from a first partner to the Gym challenge while giving familiar places another reason to return.

cards.heading: Choosing the traveller
cards.text: The choice between a boy and a girl changes who appears at the centre of the adventure. Both begin in New Bark Town and travel with the same responsibilities: raising a party, filling the Pokédex and responding to trouble along the route. This small decision makes the trainer more personal without dividing the game into separate stories. The player's own selection becomes the figure repeatedly seen entering towns, meeting rivals and stepping into battles.

cards.heading: A changing encounter
cards.text: Suicune receives a continuing presence through encounters and the pursuit of Eusine, a researcher fascinated by the legendary creature. These meetings thread another expectation through the Gym journey. Battles also announce their opponents with brief sprite animations. A movement at the start of an encounter gives an otherwise familiar image a different sense of arrival, while the turn-based decisions still depend on moves, types and the condition of the party.

cards.heading: A world shared by cable
cards.text: The collection extends beyond the creatures found in one cartridge. A Game Link Cable allows exchanges with compatible games, turning a friend's discoveries into possible additions to the player's team. Different versions provide different opportunities, and older partners can travel into the newer adventure where the trading rules permit. Johto's routes and towns therefore sit inside a wider collection whose contents reflect both time spent exploring and people willing to exchange.
